Legal framework for Internet Shutdown in India

Context: During the "Chalo Sansad" protest organised by the Cockroach Janta Party (CJP), Mobile Internet Service were shut down in parts of Central Delhi.

Provisions:

~Under Section 20(2)(b) of the Telecommunication Act, 2023 and the Telecommunications (Temporary Suspension of Services) Rules, 2024, Telecommunication services may be suspended.

~Suspension can be ordered only on the occurrence of a public emergency or in the interest of public safety on the grounds specified in that provision, and for reasons recorded in writing.

~Orders must be reasoned, published, geographically and temporarily limited and consider whether less restrictive measures are sufficient.

Under the 2024 Rules, a suspension order cannot remain in force for more than 15 days.

Supreme Court Guidelines:

~In Anuradha Bhasin v Union of India (2020), the Supreme Court linked Internet access with freedoms under Articles 19(1) (a) and 19(1)(g).

~Shutdowns must satisfy necessity and proportionality, be the least restrictive measures, and remain open to judicial review.

Suspension can be challenged in court?
Yes. Under Article 226 before a High Court and Article 32 before the Supreme Court.

Subject: 6 Urgent Demands Regarding Issues Faced by Ordinary and Migrant Workers, Refund Process, Tatkal Booking, and Train Operations.
Respected Sir,
I, Sachin Singha, an ordinary citizen and migrant worker, would like to bring to your kind attention some fundamental and serious issues of Indian Railways and the hardship faced by the common people:
Complete Cancellation of Unfair Cancellation Charges:
When we book tickets with our hard-earned money and the ticket gets automatically cancelled (Auto-cancel) by the system due to unavailability of seats, deducting a cancellation charge of ₹60 per passenger is highly unfair. Since the passenger did not get a seat, no extra charge should be deducted and the full amount must be refunded.
Rapid Refund Credit Within 12 Hours:
In cases of auto-cancellation or booking failure, the refund amount should not be held for 3–4 days; instead, it must be credited within a maximum of 12 hours. Often, due to emergency medical needs or a family bereavement, people need to return home urgently. Without timely refunds, ordinary workers do not have additional funds to book new tickets immediately. Receiving refunds quickly will enable people to book another ticket and reach their destination the very next day.
Priority and Quota Allocation for Long-Distance Passengers:
It is observed that short-distance passengers (5 to 12 hours journey) easily secure confirmed berths, whereas long-distance passengers traveling 35 to 48 hours—especially long-distance migrant workers—mostly remain on the waiting list. The seat allocation policy should be revised to prioritize long-distance travelers.
Prevention of Unfair Fines and Harassment by TTEs:
When passengers from other states or uneducated individuals commit inadvertent errors due to a lack of understanding of rules, instead of guiding them, excessive fines ranging from ₹1200 to ₹1500 are collected instead of ₹1000. Unfair fines over the prescribed train fare and harassment by TTEs must be strictly stopped.
Ensuring Punctuality and Reducing Risk of Missing Connecting Trains:
Although the schedule appears correct on the app, trains frequently run late by 1 to 2 hours in reality. Consequently, working-class passengers who need to board a connecting train face severe distress and miss their onward journeys. Ensuring punctuality in train operations is crucial.
Humane Approach Towards Common Working-Class Citizens:
The contribution of migrant workers to the country's economy and development is undeniable. A swift, permanent solution is needed to ensure that people traveling with hard-earned income do not have to travel standing due to lack of seats, and that transparency is maintained in the ticket booking and refund system.

text:
I watched #ColumEastwood MP full statement from last night on #GarvaghyRoad and I genuinely cannot believe this is the language of an elected MP in 2026.

He talks about “domination” and “triumphalism”, Orangemen walking past “our houses” to “remind us who’s in charge”, and people being “forced and penned into their houses”. Then comes this: “Why do they even want to walk down that road where they’re not wanted? I think we all know the answer.”

Do we, Colum? Because if you’re going to insinuate something about the motives of these men, stop hiding behind “we all know”. Say exactly what you’re accusing them of and bring the evidence.

Listening to that speech you’d think thousands of #Orangemen, bands and supporters were about to descend on Garvaghy Road. They’re not. #35people. Five stewards. One banner. #NoBands. #NoSupporters. Leaving #DrumcreeChurch by 8am. The proposal was for a #silent procession. That’s what is being described using the language of domination, triumphalism and people being penned into their homes.

Nobody gets to rewrite #Drumcree either. There was terrible loyalist violence and intimidation surrounding it. I won’t excuse it or pretend otherwise. But there was #IrishRepublican and #Nationalist #violence and rioting too. Police and security forces were attacked. Civilians were caught up in it. So if we’re dragging the 1990s into 2026, tell the whole bloody story. Don’t permanently cast one community as aggressors and another as victims and then hand those labels down to the next generation.

These 35 men are not responsible for everything that happened nearly 30 years ago. History is not hereditary guilt.

And history rather spoils Eastwood’s theatrical question: “Why do they even want to walk down that road?” The Drumcree church parade dates #to1807. This isn’t a route somebody invented last Tuesday to annoy Catholics. The modern dispute also has to be understood alongside Orange parades being moved away from Obins Street/The Tunnel in the 1980s and the subsequent focus on Garvaghy Road.

Residents can oppose it. Protest peacefully. Go to court. But don’t erase the history and replace it with “I think we all know the answer.” No. Say what you mean.

And then we get to the part I find impossible to ignore: the Parades Commission.

For 28 years the Orange Order 🟧🇬🇧  has been told this is the independent body that decides these disputes. Determination after determination went against #PortadownDistrict. What were Orangemen told? #Respect the process. #Accept the determination. #Obey the decision.

And they did.

Then the #HighCourt actually quashed the Commission’s recent Drumcree determination after procedural defects emerged in how it had been reached. Not every commissioner had approved its final form before it was issued. #Unionists and the Orange Order demanded resignations.

Sinn Féin’s John Finucane responded by describing unionist reaction as “tribal and triumphalist” and said that if another application was made #SinnFein would make representations to the #ParadesCommission against it. 

Think about that. Even after the High Court had quashed its decision, Sinn Fein was still prepared to go back to the same Commission and ask it to reject another Orange application.

The Orange Order then did exactly what it was supposed to do. It went back through the process. It submitted another application. The Commission considered it.

And this time the answer changed.

Suddenly the language changed too. “Reckless.” “Disgraceful.” “Shocking.” It “must not go ahead”. Eastwood says the decision “should never have been taken”, “should be overturned” and that government has a “responsibility” to ensure the procession doesn’t happen.

What changed?

Not the Orange Order’s obligation to use the process. Not the existence of the Parades Commission.

The answer changed.

Why is the 6th largest economy unable to defend the basic rights of its citizens? 

What happens when an ordinary Indian is wronged by a powerful tech company?

You appeal to the company that banned you. You explain. You submit documents. You wait. You appeal again.

And if nothing happens, you are told to approach the Government’s Grievance Appellate Committee.

And if that doesn’t help?

Go to court.

But who can actually do that?

Who has the money to hire a lawyer? Who has the time to spend months fighting? Who can afford to keep chasing authorities and corporations just to get back something that was taken away without a fair resolution?

This is the helplessness of the common Indian.

The government has institutions and procedures.

And the ordinary citizen?

They have nowhere to go.

Most people will eventually give up—not because they were wrong, but because they simply cannot afford to keep fighting.

I am fighting my WhatsApp ban. 

But what about the person who doesn’t?

What happens to their rights?

What happens to their livelihood?

What happens to their dignity?

If an ordinary citizen cannot realistically enforce their rights against a powerful corporation, what protection do those rights actually provide?

This is not just about my WhatsApp account.

It is about the millions of Indians who have no power when the system fails them.

Sound the Alarm : IFF’s First Read on MeitY's Draft IT Rules Second Amendment, 2026

New Delhi, 30 March 2026

On 30 March 2026, the Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology published proposed amendments to the IT Rules, 2021, inviting public comments by 14 April,  a comment period of barely fifteen days for changes with far reaching consequences for free speech and intermediary governance in India. We have conducted a quick review of the draft amendments. Despite being presented as "clarificatory and procedural," they represent a dangerous expansion of executive power over online speech.

We wish to state at the outset that these proposed amendments need to be immediately withdrawn and every member in our citizenry should demand their roll back and stand with the Constitution of India. These proposed amendments come at a time of fear and increased government directed censorship, especially of online political speech that includes parody and satire of the government, including the Prime Minister.

In brief the five changes are listed below:

1. Rule 3(1)(g) and 3(1)(h): Insertion of phrases within existing clauses making data retention obligations under the IT Rules additional to retention requirements under any other law.

2. Rule 3(4): Insertion of a new clause that mandates intermediary compliance with MeitY-issued clarifications, advisories, directions, SOPs, codes of practice, and guidelines, making such compliance a condition for retaining safe harbour under Section 79 of the IT Act. These are not anchored to the rule making powers of the IT Act, 2000 and provide uncanalised power to MEITY despite it stating otherwise.

3. Rule 8(1) proviso: A substitution in the proviso that expands applicability of MIB’s oversight mechanism in Part III of the rules to:  (1) intermediaries and (2) users who are not “publishers” and post/share news and current affairs content online. This oversight mechanism contains the blocking powers of MIB by way of Rule 14 (Inter-Departmental Committee), Rule 15 (Procedure for issuing directions to block), and Rule 16 (Emergency blocking provisions).

4. Rule 14(2) : A substitution that expands the scope of the IDC from hearing "complaints or grievances" to hearing "matters", including those referred by the Ministry of Information and Broadcasting.

5. Rule 14(5) : Replaces "complaints or grievances" with "the matter" in relation to IDC examination and recommendations.

A massive expansion of an unconstitutional censorship and regulatory power

First and most concerningly, Rule 3(4) creates a sweeping power for MeitY to issue binding instruments which are not anchored in law such as clarifications, advisories, directions, SOPs, codes of practice, and guidelines that intermediaries must comply with as a condition of safe harbour under Section 79 of the IT Act.

The Supreme Court's 2015 judgment in Shreya Singhal v. Union of India (2015) 5 SCC 1, remains the foundational precedent governing intermediary liability. It constrains the proposed amendments in several ways. First, the court read down Section 79(3)(b) to require that "actual knowledge" of unlawful content must come through a court order or government notification. Any Rule 3(4) making MeitY, "clarifications, advisories, directions, SOPs", lower the constitutional threshold for intermediary due diligence obligations.

Further, the settled principle in Indian administrative law, reaffirmed in Indian Express Newspapers v. Union of India (1985) 1 SCC 641 and Confederation of Ex-Servicemen Associations v. Union of India (2006) 8 SCC 399, is that delegated legislation must remain within the four corners of the parent statute.  It is important to note that the rule-making power under Section 87(1) of the IT Act is confined to, "carry[ing] out the provisions" of the Act. Section 87(2)(zg) authorizes rules for intermediary guidelines under Section 79(2), and Section 87(2)(z) for blocking procedures under Section 69A(2). Justice Chandurkar's judgement in the Kunal Kamra case clearly found the FCU amendment was not properly referable to either provision. Hence, any Rule 3(4) mandating compliance with MeitY advisories would face identical challenges since they create substantive new obligations not contemplated by Sections 79 or 87.

Even though Rule 3(4)(b)(ii) states that such, “advisories” etc. need to, “clearly specify the statutory provision or legal basis under which it is issued”, since these are not required to be published or made public there is every likelihood these will be issued with secrecy and hence may just in a tautological manner refer back to Section 79(3)(b) of the IT Act. This is similar to a logical fallacy in which it is clearly observable that a student is cheating on an exam who then claims that they may be permitted to continue cheating since they are stating at the same time they are not cheating. 

The practical effect of Rule 3(4) is that intermediaries face a perpetual compliance threat. Any failure to comply with any MeitY-issued instrument, however vague, however rapidly issued may cost them their safe harbour. The response for an intermediary is over-compliance and over-censorship.

Circumventing existing stay orders

The original proviso to Rule 8(1) stated that Part III applied to intermediaries only "for the purposes of rules 15 and 16"  i.e., content blocking directions and emergency blocking. The amended proviso now extends this to Rule 14, bringing intermediaries and user-generated news/current affairs content under the jurisdiction of the Inter-Departmental Committee.

Under Rules 9(1) and 9(3) of the 2021 IT Rules, there is a Code of Ethics compliance requirement and the three-tier grievance redressal mechanism, both of which were stayed by the Bombay High Court on 14 August 2021 as prima facie violative of Article 19(1)(a) and ultra vires the IT Act. On the oversight mechanism in Rules 14, 15, and 16, the Bombay High Court granted the petitioners to seek relief on this rule when an Inter Departmental Committee is established. The Madras High Court affirmed this stay as having pan-India effect in its order of 16 September 2021 in T.M. Krishna v. Union of India, observing that "an oversight mechanism to control the media by the government may rob the media of its independence." 

Both these cases, along with other cases challenging various provisions of the 2021 IT Rules, are now pending adjudication before the Delhi High Court.

The expansion of Rule 8(1) to cover Rules 14, 15, and 16 is an attempt to expand the blocking powers of MIB to both intermediaries and users who are not “publishers” but post news and current affairs content online. The IDC can now examine "matters" relating to user-generated news content on intermediary platforms without the Code of Ethics framework having been adjudicated as constitutional; the government effectively obtains the content oversight machinery that three High Courts found illegal, through a different procedural door.

Transforming the IDC from Grievance Body to Censorship Apparatus

The original Rule 14(2) required the IDC to hear "complaints regarding violation or contravention of the Code of Ethics." The amended version removes this requirement entirely. 

The IDC now hears:
(a) grievances arising from decisions at Level I or II; or
(b) "matters" referred to by the Ministry.

Clause (b) is unconstrained since, (a) there is no requirement that the "matter" arise from a complaint, (b) no requirement that the "matter" relate to a Code of Ethics violation; and (c) no requirement that the affected party be heard before the referral. The Ministry of Information and Broadcasting can, on its own motion, refer any content-related "matter" to the IDC. 

The cumulative effect of the amendments to Rules 8 and 14 is to reconstruct the oversight machinery that the Bombay and Madras High Courts found constitutionally suspect, in a form designed to evade the existing interim orders. The IDC, previously limited to the three-tier complaints process under the stayed Rules 9(3), 12, and 13 framework, now operates as a free-standing censorship committee that can take up "matters" referred by the executive.

Increased user surveillance through mandatory data retention directions

Insertion of phrases within existing clauses making data retention obligations under the IT Rules additional to retention requirements under any other law. For instance, the mandatory data retention of user data beyond 180 days within Rule 3(1)(g) and 3(1)(h) may be prescribed for longer periods and other purposes raising risks of surveillance and even potentially data leaks of sensitive data that is stored for longer periods of time. Government mandates for data retention as to their legal authority and hence period of retention will be beyond those contained under the IT Act.

Statement on MeitY's notice to WhatsApp over the "usernames" feature

The Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology (MeitY) has sent WhatsApp a notice about the usernames feature it announced on 29 June 2026. The notice asks the company to explain, within three days, why regulatory action should not be taken against it "for launching a feature that may increase cybercrimes", and it directs the company "not to roll out this feature until the consultation on this point is achieved to the satisfaction of the Government". The Internet Freedom Foundation is concerned that the notice has no clear basis in law. It is an attempt by the executive to decide what a company may build and ship, which no statute permits.

The notice treats the launch of a lawful feature as a wrong the company must justify. That reverses the ordinary position especially given the absence of any clear legal power that exists. MeitY does not name any provision that lets it approve a product feature before release or order one withdrawn, because there is none, and the provisions it does cite do not supply that power.

Section 79 of the IT Act, 2000 is a safe harbour that protects an intermediary from liability for what its users post, so long as it observes due diligence. It decides when a platform can be held liable. It is not a power for MeitY to decide what features the platform may offer. Sections 66C and 66D punish identity theft and cheating by personation. They are criminal offences, tried by courts, aimed at the person who steals an identity, not at the maker of a tool that a third party misuses. Also, on MeitY's logic, a telecom operator could be told not to sell SIM cards because SIM cards are used in almost every online fraud. 

Rule 3(1)(b), Rule 3(2) and Rule 4 of the IT Rules, 2021 are due diligence and grievance obligations and cannot be converted into a licensing scheme. Section 69A, the one provision that lets MeitY control what appears online, permits the blocking of specific information through a set procedure. It says nothing about which features a company may build. Further the IT Rules, 2021 are subordinate legislation made under Sections 79 and 87 of the IT Act, and subordinate rules cannot travel beyond the parent statute (Ajoy Kumar Banerjee v. Union of India). If a rule cannot exceed the Act, a letter certainly cannot. The power to require prior permission for a feature is not in the Act, not in the Rules, and cannot be created by a notice. 

MeitY has tried this before. In March 2024 it told the same large intermediaries, among them AI Companies, to obtain its explicit permission before deploying under-tested AI models. That was criticised as an overreach that sought to build a licensing mechanism with no empowering provision in the IT Act, and within a fortnight MeitY withdrew it and dropped the permission requirement. This notice repeats the move for a single feature and goes further, because it names one company, sets a three-day clock, and bars the launch until MeitY is satisfied. 

This matters beyond WhatsApp. A power asserted against one company by letter can be turned on any company and any feature. On this reasoning MeitY could tell a browser not to switch on a privacy setting by default, or a payments app not to add a login method, each time until it was content. The notice also invokes traceability, through Rule 4(2) of the IT Rules, 2021 and the identification of the "first originator" of a message. Rule 4(2) has been challenged as exceeding its parent provision and resting on no law made by Parliament, and that challenge is pending before the Delhi High Court. Raising it against a feature meant to share fewer identifiers fits a pattern. 

We ask MeitY to state the exact provision of law under which this notice, and the direction to halt the roll-out, has been issued, and to withdraw that direction. It should stop using Section 79 and the contested traceability rule as leverage to control product design and to reverse features that improve privacy. Impersonation and fraud are real risks, but they are met by enforcing the criminal law against those who commit them, and by open processes that rest on identified legal powers. They are not met by MeitY deciding, in private and by letter, what features Indians may use. That is a licence raj for software features.

The framework brings together the IT Act, 2000, Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita (BNS), 2023, IT Rules, 2021, the 2026 IT Rules amendments, and the IndiaAI Governance Guidelines to strengthen digital safety and platform accountability.

Key highlights:

🔹 Mandatory AI Labelling: Platforms must clearly label AI-generated or synthetic content with traceable metadata so users can identify manipulated content and prevent deception.

🔹 Fastest Takedown Timelines Yet: Removal of unlawful content after a valid government or court notice has been reduced from 36 hours to just 3 hours. Grievance redressal timelines have also been tightened—from 72 hours to 36 hours, and 24 hours to 2 hours for sensitive content such as nudity, impersonation and similar categories.

🔹 IT Act, 2000: Covers penalties for computer-related offences, identity theft (Sec. 66C), online impersonation (66D), privacy violations (66E), publishing obscene or sexually explicit content (Secs. 67 & 67A), empowers blocking of unlawful content under Sec. 69A, removal directions under Sec. 79, and enables police investigation under Secs. 78 & 80.

🔹 Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023: Covers cheating by personation (Sec. 319), forgery through false electronic records (Sec. 336), spreading false reports or misinformation causing public mischief (Sec. 353), and organised cybercrime involving deepfake content (Sec. 111).

🔹 Strict Platform Obligations: Intermediaries must not host or share content that infringes rights, invades privacy, promotes hate or violence, harms children, violates intellectual property, misleads users about message origin, knowingly spreads false information, impersonates individuals (including using AI), threatens India's sovereignty, security or public order, or violates any applicable law.

🔹 Greater Accountability for Social Media Platforms: Significant Social Media Intermediaries (SSMIs) must assist law enforcement in tracing originators of serious content, deploy automated tools to detect unlawful content, publish compliance reports, appoint grievance and compliance officers, maintain India-based compliance infrastructure, and provide user verification, appeals and fair hearing mechanisms.

🔹 Zero Tolerance for Harmful AI: Platforms are now explicitly required to prevent AI-generated child sexual abuse material, non-consensual intimate imagery, deepfakes, AI impersonation, harmful synthetic media and other unlawful AI-generated content using reasonable technical measures and automated detection systems.

🔹 Legal Consequences: Failure to comply with the IT Rules can result in intermediaries losing their Section 79 safe-harbour protection, exposing them to prosecution and legal action under applicable laws.

🔹 Robust Enforcement Ecosystem: The framework will be enforced through Grievance Appellate Committees (GACs), the Indian Cyber Crime Coordination Centre (I4C), the SAHYOG Portal, the National Cyber Crime Reporting Portal, and law enforcement agencies. Citizens can report cybercrime and deepfakes through the National Cyber Crime Reporting Portal, with Helpline 1930 available for cyber fraud complaints.

🔹 Responsible AI Development: Under the IndiaAI Mission, the government is funding indigenous AI safety projects, including Saakshya (IIT Jodhpur & IIT Madras), AI Vishleshak, and IIT Kharagpur's Real-Time Voice Deepfake Detection System, alongside the India AI Governance Guidelines to promote safe, trusted and responsible AI deployment.

The message is clear: AI innovation is welcome, but deepfakes, impersonation, misinformation, child exploitation, and unlawful synthetic content will face significantly stricter regulation, faster takedowns, and stronger legal consequences than ever before.

The Union Government and Delhi Police have told Delhi High Court X is liable to lose its safe harbour protection in India because it failed to act against Rana Ayyub’s offensive tweets about Hindu deities and Savarkar.

Here’s @barandbench report on what transpired in court:

The Government has said that the police had issued notices in September 2025 and December 2025, requesting X to take down Ayyub’s posts. The Government said that in January 2025, a trial court ordered registration of an FIR against Ayyub over these posts.

The police notices and trial court order constitute “actual knowledge” under the Information Technology (Intermediary Guidelines and Digital Media Ethics Code) Rules, 2021, triggering a statutory obligation on X to act expeditiously and remove such unlawful content, the High Court has been told.

It added that as X failed to act despite “actual knowledge” the safe harbour protection available to it is liable to be withdrawn.

Notably, the High Court had on April 8, 2026 observed that these tweets (made between 2013-2017) were derogatory and communal. 

After the hearing, the Delhi Police sent a request to MEITY to block the content and the request is under consideration, the Court has been told.

Meanwhile, X has also filed a response in the High Court and said that the petition should be directed against Rana Ayyub (the uploader of the content) and not X. 

It also also directions to Delhi Police to follow the  2009 Blocking Rules and issue a blocking order under Section 69A of the IT Act.

Rana Ayyub's lawyers told the Court today that the writ petition was not maintainable. 

The HC has granted Ayyub two weeks time to file a reply in the case, including on the issue of maintainability.

Preface

Over the past few years, the AI industry has been constantly adding.

More parameters, longer contexts, more GPUs, larger data centers. Models are increasingly becoming black boxes capable of containing half of the internet, and we have also become increasingly accustomed to using scale to explain intelligence.

But recently I saw a completely opposite approach: someone lets a neural network finish training, then throws away the weights, matrix multiplication, and even the “neurons” in the conventional sense, leaving behind only a few dozen AND, OR, XOR, and NAND gates.

手羽先｜国産LLMを作る人
@Tebasaki_lab
·
7 Sep

(Translated from Japanese)

【Shocking】World’s First?! Playing Mario with Just 29 Logic Gates?!

The results from our team-developed logic gate-based AI library in the Untrodden IT project are coming in insanely hot🔥🔥 We’ve finally started controlling Mario!!!

We don’t know yet if we can clear it, but

29 logic gates have already started controlling Mario. The author honestly says that they still don’t know whether it can clear the game; their longer Japanese post also reviews the research path of DLGN, convolution, recurrence, and Cellular Automata.

Another Builder compressed a driving strategy into 13 ordinary logic gates, then synthesized it into 21 NAND gates and burned it into Tapeout Circuit #279; Microduck then separated steering and memory into two Circuits and combined them.

My first reaction was not, “on-chain AGI is here.”

Quite the opposite. These things are still very far from an LLM. What really interests me is another question:

If the experience learned by AI can ultimately be compressed into an extremely small, deterministic, public circuit that anyone can verify, then perhaps Tapeout has, for the first time, found a truly natural interface between AI and on-chain hardware.

Not moving training on-chain, and not having blockchain replace GPUs.

But letting AI learn off-chain, and letting Tapeout burn the learned rules into a fixed form.

This is smaller than “running a model on-chain,” and it may also be more important.

⸻

1. What exactly is this kind of network?

Its name is Differentiable Logic Gate Network, or DLGN.

A node in a traditional neural network usually receives many inputs, multiplies them by weights, adds them together, and then passes them through an activation function.

Logic gate networks have none of this. Each node has only two inputs and executes one of the 16 possible two-input Boolean functions, such as AND, OR, XOR, and NAND.

The problem is that logic gates are discrete.

AND is AND. It will not suddenly become 0.37 AND + 0.63 XOR because of gradient descent.

So researchers did something very clever, and very “AI”: during training, they first tell a benevolent little lie.

The logic gates, which originally could only receive 0 and 1, are temporarily relaxed into continuous functions over [0,1]. Each node does not immediately choose a particular gate. Instead, it retains a set of probabilities, which are gradually adjusted through backpropagation.

After training, the lie ends.

Each node keeps only the gate with the highest probability.

Floating-point numbers, softmax, gradients, and Adam all leave the stage. What remains is a pure Boolean circuit.

“After training, the resulting network is discretized to a hard logic gate network by choosing the logic gate with the highest probability.”
— Petersen et al., Deep Differentiable Logic Gate Networks

So this is not the same thing as a BNN, or Binary Neural Network.

A BNN is still a weight-based network; it simply compresses weights or activations into ±1 and uses XNOR and popcount for acceleration.

A logic gate network has no traditional weights. What it learns is exactly which gate should be placed at each position.

5. Microduck goes one step further: Circuits can be combined, but memory isn’t truly on-chain yet

Microduck’s structure is more interesting.

#281 uses 39 NAND gates to process 14-bit virtual depth and target direction and output steering.

#282 uses 22 NAND gates + 3 LATCHes to add a fixed steering-memory rule.

CircuitGraph then connects the two separately taped-out Circuits.

This proves two important directions:

Learned policies can be independently taped out.

State rules can exist as a second Circuit and be combined with the first.

But the public page also makes it clear:

Sensing, walking, physics, and the upstream ONNX gait model remain in the browser or locally.

In on-chain mode, each step is simply a read-only CircuitGraph call.

Trial memory is passed from the browser to the next step.

The contract’s callerState is never written.

Refreshing the page clears it.

So for now, it is a combined control prototype with LATCH semantics, not a machine with persistent on-chain memory.

This distinction may sound disappointing, but it is actually more valuable.

Because it exposes the next engineering problem for Tapeout:

Not building a bigger model, but properly separating the responsibilities of policy, state, account, and executor.

⸻

6. DiffLogic CA: potentially a better future for Tapeout than an “on-chain LLM”

Google’s DiffLogic CA conducted a series of very elegant experiments.

It first trained a model to learn the local rules of Conway’s Game of Life.

A 3×3 neighborhood has only 2^9 = 512 possible inputs.

The training set covered all configurations, and the resulting hard circuit could generate gliders, blocks, and oscillators on larger grids.

The project reported 336 active gates.

Even more surprising was the checkerboard experiment:

An 8-bit cell state running on a 16×16 grid for 20 steps.

After training, there were 22 active gates.

After further pruning, only six remained, one of which was redundant, ultimately leaving the equivalent of five effective logic gates.

When the grid and time were both scaled by 4×, it still worked.

Even when local cells were damaged, it could maintain or recover the pattern.

This can easily create the imagination of “programmable life on-chain.”

But don’t rush.

A rule having only five gates does not mean that running 64×64 cells for 80 steps also costs only five gates.

The total execution cost is closer to:

number of cells × number of steps × cost per rule execution.

This is also where DiffLogic CA is most interesting to combine with Tapeout:

The same small Circuit can be reused on a large scale, but reuse is not free.

The most realistic path right now is not to start with lizards, colorful patterns, or “life on-chain.”

Start with extremely small state machines.

If this path works, Tapeout may not only preserve functions. It could begin preserving rules that can repeatedly grow through time.

This is much slower and much harder than “putting a large model on-chain.”

But at least it is facing a real problem, rather than arranging a date between two buzzwords: AI and blockchain.

7. How developers should get started

For the first project, don’t touch image classification, and definitely don’t touch LLMs.

Choose a task with no more than 16 input bits, no more than 4 output bits, and one whose entire input space can be fully verified.

Step 1: Define the inputs before writing the model

Every bit must have a clearly defined name, threshold, unit, order, and missing-value rule.

The external world is not naturally Boolean.

How sensors, prices, identities, and events become bits is itself a trust boundary.

Step 2: Split the data by environment

Do not randomly place adjacent frames into train and test.

For driving tasks, split by track or episode.

For robots, split by scene.

For Agent permissions, split by assets, addresses, and anomaly types.

Step 3: Train a small model first

Basic DLGN, Gumbel LGN, Light DLGN, AP, evolutionary search, or even manually written rules are all acceptable.

The training algorithm should not become a matter of protocol ideology.

Tapeout ultimately cares about the hard circuit you deliver and the evidence supporting it.

Step 4: Report both soft and hard performance

Only the hard score represents the machine that will actually be executed in the future.

Step 5: Synthesize, don’t simply translate

Do not directly replace every DLGN node with a NAND gate.

A reliable toolchain should keep at least six layers of semantics separate.

The Boolean IR should first preserve the semantics of:

NOT
AND
OR
XOR
constants
inputs
outputs
state

Then perform:

constant propagation
dead-code elimination
structural hashing
common subexpression sharing
critical-path analysis

Only afterward should it be handed to EDA tools such as Yosys/ABC for global optimization and NAND technology mapping.

The reason is simple:

Adding up the cost of individual gates does not equal the cost of the globally synthesized network.

Multiple nodes may share the same inverter.

Dead branches can be completely removed.

A seemingly expensive XOR may become cheaper after global Boolean factoring.

For stateful logic, it should be explicitly represented as:

next state = F(current state, input)

Step 6: Prove that the compiler didn’t break the model

For small input domains, use exhaustive testing.

For large input domains, construct a miter circuit and use SAT/SMT, property tests, and counterexample replay.

Ideally, do not verify only the final step. Check layer by layer.

Here we must also distinguish three things that are often mixed together:

Equivalence proof only shows that the compiler faithfully reproduced the hard model. It does not prove that the hard model itself learned the correct behavior, nor does it automatically prove that the model is safe.

Step 7: Only then Tape Out

First create a local replica.

Then perform read-only evaluation.

Then enter the public Arena.

Only afterward should you consider persistent state, Containers, and external assets.

The complete development process, manifest fields, NAND lowering, testing, and submission checklist have been organized separately into a developer guide so that the tutorial does not swallow this article.

⸻

8. How should PoD accommodate learned Circuits?

The most fascinating part of PoD (Proof of Design) right now is that it does not reward “whoever occupies the position first.”

It rewards the current best design with strictly lower cost under the same public task.

Later builders can surpass it, while older designs remain in the verified pool.

This philosophy fits logic synthesis extremely well.

But machine-learning accuracy cannot simply be inserted into the cost formula.

Open tasks have no absolute correctness, and public test sets can be overfitted.

A more reasonable structure is:

Meet the performance requirement first, then compete on cost.

The same task could have 90%, 95%, and 99% performance tiers.

Within the same tier, builders could compete based on:

NAND count
LATCH count
depth
bytes
worst-case state-update cost

An agent can complete a task and still spend more than the result is worth. Economic governors set budgets, limit retries, and escalate when costs exceed the value at stake. Autonomy needs a spending policy. https://t.co/0vDFE7V58G

I’ve put the complaint, the exhibits and the older company records together because I want people to be able to follow this case without having to piece it together from screenshots and replies.

That includes both sides. Korra says he received court documents, denies the allegations and says none of this happened. His denial needs to be included.

X filed its lawsuit against Immortal Snail LLC on September 28, 2026, in the Northern District of Texas. The case number is 4:26-cv-01254. Immortal Snail is the only named defendant in the federal case. Being mentioned in the complaint doesn’t automatically make someone else a defendant.

This is a civil lawsuit about contracts, suspended accounts and arbitration. X wants to stop the arbitration brought by Snail and is suing for breach of contract. There’s no judgment in the material I’ve reviewed establishing the bribery, unauthorized-access or impersonation allegations as proven. The complaint doesn’t bring a standalone RICO claim either, although RICO comes up in an earlier letter.

The complaint itself is 31 pages. The ECF 1 package I reviewed runs to 288 pages, including the cover sheet, index and 25 exhibits. Those exhibits matter because they also include Snail’s account, letters from its lawyers, contracts and commercial records. This package isn’t the entire, up-to-date court file.

One document deserves particular attention: the January 12, 2026 letter from their own lawyers.

Kevin C. Kaplan and Christopher E. Cheek, of Coffey Burlington, say they represent Immortal Snail, Moonrail Limited B.V. and Ossi Ketola. They describe Ketola as the “principal and owner” of both companies. The letter is part of Snail’s arbitration claim, included in Exhibit 25, pages 17–18.

If you have a claim or ongoing proceedings against Ketola involving Duel or CSGOEmpire, that’s a document worth putting in front of your lawyer. It gives them a specific statement from his stated representatives to consider when looking at ownership, corporate relationships and who belongs in your case. The separate companies, directors and representatives have to be considered alongside that statement.

The letter doesn’t settle personal liability, give ownership percentages or establish that one company is a subsidiary of the other. It also doesn’t prove that the companies are fictitious or their directors are acting as fronts. What it does record is how those lawyers described their clients and Ketola’s ownership.

The platforms’ own terms identify the companies:

Duel: Immortal Snail LLC, Nevis, registration L22982.
CSGOEmpire: Moonrail Limited B.V., Curaçao, registration 148182.
Payments for Moonrail may be handled by JHOLT LTD, Cyprus, registration HE393291, under an agreement between the two companies.

Moonrail also appears in DUEL’s trademark records. The official Israeli register lists it as the owner of trademark 374583, registered on May 5, 2025. In Canada, Moonrail filed DUEL application 2342187 on August 6, 2024. The Canadian record names David S. Lipkus of Lipkus Law LLP as the trademark agent and records the application as abandoned under section 36 on July 17, 2026.

That abandonment concerns the Canadian application. It doesn’t mean every DUEL trademark was cancelled or the platform stopped operating. And these records describe different jobs: owning a trademark, operating a platform, processing payments and representing a trademark applicant aren’t interchangeable roles.

The account history in X’s complaint starts in 2024, before the purchases people are discussing.

X alleges that on March 25, 2024, Ketola and Snail took control of an account using @duel, changed its email to a Moonrail mailbox and used it to promote a casino. X says it suspended the account on March 27, after which attempts to recover it involved intermediaries and access to employees. [Paragraphs 36–39.]

X also alleges that Ketola and CSGOEmpire were involved in an intrusion into @CSGORoll reported in April 2024. It cites a livestream in which, according to the complaint, Ketola celebrated what happened, mentioned “Sticky Hand” and said he worked for him. I haven’t authenticated the original video. X says it suspended @JNSAST the following day after reports of targeted harassment, disclosure of personal information and threats. [Paragraphs 28–29.]

The complaint goes on to describe what X calls bribery and unauthorized account reinstatements. It alleges that internal information about @duel was obtained in June 2024 and usernames were changed to move @monarch to another account. It also says an employee photographed internal information in July after a $1,500 offer and was fired. Further reinstatements through contractors and further suspensions followed, according to X. [Paragraphs 39, 40 and 44–49.]

There’s a company letter in this part of the file too. Exhibit 3 contains Moonrail’s July 9, 2024 authorization for Dušan Pećić to represent it. The names beneath the signatures are Lorenza Godett and Christopher van Rosberg, acting for Xecutive Corporate Management B.V., which is identified as a director of Moonrail. HLTV also named Pećić as CSGOEmpire’s marketing manager in March 2024.

The letter authorizes representation. It doesn’t authorize hacking, bribery or threats, or show that its signatories knew about the conduct X alleges.

The dates also need to stay as written. X dates Pećić’s appeal to June 28, 2024, but the authorization letter is dated July 9. Paragraph 47 then dates the rejection to July 13, 2025. I’m not going to quietly change those dates to make them line up.

Haci Isik appears as an intermediary. X says he was engaged in December 2024 to recover @duel and looked for insiders willing to reactivate or suspend accounts for money. It says he later tried to buy the handle directly, presenting an esports and FPS gaming project in February 2025. That’s X’s description of the discussions and their purpose. [Paragraphs 41–43.]

Paragraph 43 names two different payers: according to X, Moonrail paid for @duel_temp’s Premium subscription, while Immortal Snail paid for @duel itself. The person negotiating, the subscription payer and the handle buyer have different roles in that account. We don’t have the full negotiation or complete banking records in this package.

The acquisition documents total $480,000:

A $300,000 invoice for @Duel, dated March 24, 2025.
An $80,000 invoice for @Monarch, dated April 16.
A $100,000 receipt for @Castle, paid on June 3.

Snail says it paid all three. But two documents are invoices and one is a receipt, so I’m not calling them three bank payment confirmations. The @Castle receipt says “Crypto.” It gives no wallet, network, asset or transaction hash to trace. [Exhibit 25, pp. 13–15.]

A handle can move between accounts. The 2024 events and the 2025 purchases don’t establish that one person continuously owned one underlying account.

Then there’s the Grizzly section shown in the screenshot.

X describes Grizzly as a former CSGOEmpire Product Manager who fell out with Ketola. It alleges that Ketola and Snail accessed one of his accounts without authorization in February 2025, after he published internal conversations. [Paragraph 30.]

According to X, the Discord and Telegram conversations discussed accessing Israeli government email accounts and using them to ask platforms to remove competitors’ accounts, including CSGORoll. The complaint also describes discussions about wording those requests to make them look like legitimate official requests.

The original emails and their headers aren’t in the package I reviewed, and I haven’t independently verified who controlled those mailboxes. None of this establishes involvement by the Israeli government.

Paragraph 31 quotes Grizzly claiming to have more than 6.5 GB of chat exports and other evidence. In that quoted post, he said the material included plans to disclose relatives’ personal information and references to physical attacks against Stake. He also said he feared for his life and was looking for a journalist to receive the files.

The full archive isn’t here. His statement that he had it doesn’t tell us whether he delivered it to X, a journalist or an authority.

Paragraph 32 describes a video conversation between “Gr1zzly” and “Monarch,” whom X identifies as Ketola. X attributes to Monarch references to Bosnian mafia contacts, plans for kidnappings and possible murders, obtaining personal information, services involving violence and statements about mutilations.

Those are exceptionally serious allegations. I haven’t authenticated the original video, and I don’t have independent evidence establishing that the acts described were carried out. I’m reporting what X attributes to that conversation.

Paragraph 33 describes another conversation, on Telegram, about using government emails to get accounts removed, with language involving escalation and violence. Here the complaint calls the participant “Ossi” and says he is presumably Ossi Ketola. “Presumably” is in the document. It stays in this account too.

X says one of Grizzly’s accounts was taken over, had its biography changed from “Ex-CSGOEmpire” to a message saying it had been seized by @theJNSAST, then was used to promote Duel. It also cites @monarchlawyer announcing an account takeover. A username containing “lawyer” doesn’t establish that the person using it is one. [Paragraph 34.]

Korra expressly denies these events in the post being quoted. That denial belongs alongside the allegations. I also couldn’t retrieve the original links in footnotes 15–18 in readable form, so the complaint and screenshots aren’t a substitute for authenticating the underlying material.

X makes a technical claim as well. Footnote 15 says @fastschitzobear, @CSGOEmpire, @CSGOEmpireV2, @duel and @monarch used the same Known Device Token. X treats that as evidence of previous access through the same device or browser and an indication of collaboration. Paragraph 50 also refers to matches involving devices, software, identifiers, cookies and financial accounts.

The complete logs and dates needed to check that conclusion aren’t in the package. A shared device doesn’t tell us who wrote a particular message, or whether the overlap happened before or after an account takeover.

There are further allegations about accounts critical of the business.

Paragraph 35 describes a trademark complaint with allegedly manipulated documents against a former CSGOEmpire social media manager. That role shouldn’t automatically be treated as the Product Manager role attributed to Grizzly. In paragraph 52, X alleges that Isik offered in June 2025 to find insiders who would suspend accounts critical of Ketola and his companies. These remain allegations in the material reviewed.

X says it suspended @duel, @monarch and @castle, along with related accounts, around October 21, 2025. It alleges that requests impersonating a US law firm followed, as did a $300,000 offer to an employee to reactivate accounts. Exhibits 1 and 2 contain the November letters X disputes. Paragraph 56 doesn’t give the exact date of the alleged offer.

There are two different $300,000 figures here. The first is the invoiced purchase price for @Duel. The second is an alleged bribe in a later incident. They shouldn’t be merged.

Paragraph 58 describes a May 2026 request that X says impersonated the Malaysian police, followed by complaints in India. The exhibits show the request fields, but they don’t authenticate the senders. I’m leaving out the names of people who may themselves have been impersonated.

X mentions Arya A. when linking an email identifier used in requests with one in billing documents. That is X’s attribution. It doesn’t establish a company position or authorship of every communication.

Snail’s side is in the file too, and it deserves to be read.

Its arbitration claim says it paid for the handles and then lost access without an adequate explanation, harming its business, reputation and commercial expectations. It wants the accounts restored and compensation. It also raises possible interference by competitors or an X shareholder connected to competitors. The material I reviewed neither names that shareholder nor establishes that theory. [Exhibit 25, pp. 4–8.]

Snail started arbitration in April 2026. X says the relevant contracts require disputes to go to Texas courts. Mohamed F. Sweify was appointed arbitrator in July. Kaplan and Cheek attended an August preliminary hearing; X had said it wouldn’t participate and maintained that position. The arbitration order put jurisdiction first.

Part of the dispute is which terms apply. The 2024 handle-transfer terms select a Texas forum, reserve suspension rights and include a $100 limit on liability. Snail relies on the October 2025 Marketplace terms, which include arbitration subject to US residency. How those terms apply here is a question in the case, not something this post resolves.

X’s September letter mentioned possible legal actions, including RICO. That doesn’t turn this into a filed RICO claim, a criminal prosecution or an established FBI investigation.

The federal complaint names Caitlin A. Halpern and Lauryn E. Bennett of Gibbs & Bruns, and Charles W. Fillmore of Brown Pruitt, as X’s lawyers. The public docket records the case’s reassignment to Reed O’Connor on September 30. A lawyer’s representation of a party doesn’t make them responsible for the conduct being disputed.

The older company records help explain the business relationships. They need to be read with their own limits: these are supplied historical copies, and I haven’t independently certified every file’s authenticity or confirmed its official receipt. The X lawsuit doesn’t authenticate the rest of the archive.

An August 2023 organizational chart shows Ossi owning 100% of Moonrail and Moonrail owning 100% of JHOLT. That tells us what the chart records at that time; it isn’t a current ownership certificate. [D026.]

Moonrail’s shareholders’ register goes further back. The copy marked D027 reproduces a certification dated July 29, 2024. It records Xecutive Corporate Management B.V. subscribing for all 10,000 shares on October 1, 2018, then transferring them the next day. That initial shareholding is a separate role from its later corporate administration work.

The register lists these corporate holdings from October 2, 2018, and their later transfers:

JPellikka Oy, Finland, 2881789-9: 13.65%, later recorded under Day Star Enterprises OÜ, Estonia, 14630609.
Hiirijoki & Partners Oy, Finland, 2887371-9: 12.50%, later recorded under Rotten Apples OÜ, Estonia, 14631261.
create.repeat Oy, Finland, 2662670-6: 13.65%, later recorded under Simple Holdings OÜ, Estonia, 14635334.

It dates those three transfers to December 17, 2018. It then records Ketola, who already held 44.80%, acquiring the remaining 55.20% on November 13, 2019. That remaining stake consists of the three company holdings totaling 39.80%, plus an individual holding of 15.40%.

Those entries don’t tell us the purchase price or show the payments. They also don’t make those companies current owners of Duel. [D027, pp. 3–4.]

The Estonian public register confirms the companies’ identities and gives these dates:

Day Star: registered December 21, 2018; deleted from the register August 13, 2021.
Rotten Apples: registered December 27, 2018; deleted September 8, 2021.
Simple Holdings: registered January 4, 2019; deleted November 26, 2021.

All three registration dates are later than the December 17 transfer date in Moonrail’s book. That needs an explanation from the underlying documents. I can’t resolve the legally effective transfer dates from these records or call the discrepancy proof of forgery. The public company records establish those companies’ existence; the link to Moonrail’s shares comes from the supplied shareholders’ register.

Finland’s register also shows that JPellikka Oy became Veivi Ventures Oy on January 18, 2023. A later name change doesn’t establish a present-day stake in Moonrail.

There’s more on the earlier funding in a November 14, 2025 letter addressed to the Curaçao Gaming Authority. Moonrail says its initial funding came from Ketola’s earlier business activities through Global Vault oy and the distribution of that company’s assets after liquidation.

Global Vault’s Finnish registration number is 2793380-4. It was registered on November 9, 2016, and dissolved on April 1, 2019. The register confirms those facts. The explanation connecting its funds to Moonrail comes from Moonrail’s letter; it isn’t bank verification and doesn’t establish that Global Vault operated CSGOEmpire. [D050, pp. 1–3.]

The historical PRH/Virre extract issued on August 14, 2026 lists Ossi Eemeli Ketola as Global Vault’s board member and managing director from November 9, 2016 to July 5, 2018. It lists Satu Maarit Ketola as a deputy board member over the same period, and Lari Hiirijoki as a procurist, meaning a holder of a commercial power of attorney, from November 2017. His later appointment as liquidator was registered on July 5, 2018.

Those are documented business roles. They don’t establish family relationships or positions for those other individuals at today’s operators. [Global Vault PRH/Virre extract, pp. 1–3.]

The January 18, 2019 liquidator’s report in D050 identifies Ketola as holding all 100 shares and the rights to Global Vault’s asset distribution. Lari Hiirijoki signs as liquidator. This adds to the ownership and funding history, but it still doesn’t supply the records of transfers between the people and companies involved. [D050, pp. 10–11.]

There’s a one-year difference between two documents that I’m keeping visible. Moonrail’s November 2025 letter says Ketola owned 100% of Moonrail from November 13, 2018. The shareholders’ register puts his purchase of the final 55.20% on November 13, 2019. I don’t have enough to settle which date is correct.

The same letter gives Moonrail’s licensing account: Cyberluck N.V. in 2018, Antillephone N.V. in 2021, then the Gaming Control Board/Curaçao Gaming Authority framework. That is Moonrail’s account of its sublicensing and licensing history. It doesn’t establish permission to operate everywhere, and it can’t simply be applied to Immortal Snail. [D050, p. 1.]

The February 2025 assessment in the archive identifies missing documentation and recommends conditions covering management identification, anti-money-laundering measures, responsible gambling, territorial access and media policy. These are recommendations, not a sanction or proof that every proposed condition was imposed. [D029.]

A later business plan, identified in the archive as October 30, 2025, names Irene Rosenblatt as CEO, Matt Tanner as CFO and Sampsa Saarela as CTO. It names Rokas Daugirdas as compliance manager and Pearl Reiph as MLRO, the money-laundering reporting role. Xecutive is described as the board, with the CEO responsible for daily operations and reporting to it. Those are the roles this historical plan gives them. I haven’t verified that they still hold them, and the titles don’t prove involvement in X’s allegations. [D041, pp. 1–2 and 4–5.]

Moonrail’s advertising policy is worth reading in full as well. Version 1.0, dated May 29, 2025, requires prior advertising review, influencer agreements, sponsorship disclosure and territorial controls. It prohibits presenting gambling as a solution to financial difficulties, associating it with violence or dangerous behavior, and using content or influencers that appeal to minors. Advertising materials require compliance approval. Moonrail and its agents are also prohibited from offering players credit or loans to gamble. [D037, pp. 4–6.]

Those are written rules for Moonrail at that date. To assess a particular campaign against them, we’d still need to check the campaign itself, when it ran and which policy applied. Having a policy doesn’t tell us how it was followed in every case.

The archive also contains an August 1, 2025 response attributed to Xecutive on Moonrail’s behalf about Coffeezilla. It denies bribery. It says former managers proposed investigating a competitor without senior authorization, denies asking anyone to suppress or change coverage of Moonrail, and says the people who acted without authorization were removed. They aren’t named. The letter describes the owner as providing strategic guidance, separate from operational campaigns. That response needs to accompany the allegation. [D038.]

The August and November 2025 letters both present Xecutive Corporate Management B.V. as a director of Moonrail. Their signature blocks name Analissa Heiland and Lorenza Godett as its representatives. That establishes how they are presented in those letters, not participation in the alleged conduct. These letters and the other historical copies remain subject to the authenticity and date limitations explained above. [D038, p. 2; D050, p. 2.]

The regulatory decisions have their own official sources.

Spain’s decision ES/2025/011 imposes a €5 million fine and a four-year disqualification from conducting gambling activities on Moonrail for operating without the required Spanish authorization. It identifies CSGOEmpire and orders the activity to stop. The DGOJ announced the sanction in November 2025. I haven’t verified whether it was paid or the outcome of any appeals.

Sweden prohibited Moonrail from providing gambling without the required license in a decision dated November 2, 2023. Denmark’s official list includes https://t.co/wm4kIZPtIu among the domains blocked by court order in July 2023.

Those decisions apply to the countries and dates they cover. They don’t prove X’s allegations of bribery or unauthorized access. A declared Curaçao or Anjouan license doesn’t establish permission to operate in every other market either.

For people with disputes over balances or affiliate earnings, the terms themselves also matter. CSGOEmpire’s terms, marked as updated on July 7, 2026, promise withdrawals even when an account is closed and, where necessary, compensation for unclaimed referral earnings or rewards. They also contain exceptions and restrictions for abuse, self-referrals, dormant accounts and reversed trades. Any particular withholding needs to be checked against the terms that applied, the clause relied on and the account records. The page alone doesn’t prove a breach in someone’s case.

I also need to be open about my own position. I’ve filed a police complaint over a separate dispute. It records my allegations; it isn’t a judgment proving them. X’s case doesn’t settle my claims either. I’m leaving out amounts that still need reconciliation and keeping the two proceedings separate.

What we have here is a civil complaint, Snail’s arbitration claim, commercial records, a letter from lawyers describing Ketola’s ownership of both operators, historical company documents and official regulatory decisions. The most serious allegations in the complaint haven’t been established as proven in the material I’ve reviewed.

If I’ve got a document, page or date wrong, point me to it. I’ll correct it. I’ll also include responses supported by documents.

The Centre has issued a notice to messaging platform Telegram, directing it to take concrete measures within 15 days to curb the widespread circulation of pirated films, OTT content and other copyrighted audio-visual material on its platform.

The notice, issued by the Ministry of Information and Broadcasting (I&B) on July 4, asks Telegram to strengthen its mechanisms for detecting, reporting, disabling access to and removing infringing content. The move is aimed at safeguarding India's creator economy, film industry, broadcasters, OTT platforms, producers and distributors.

The government has also instructed the platform to take action against repeat offenders, including channels, groups, bots, accounts, administrators and associated entities involved in the dissemination of pirated content.

In addition, Telegram has been asked to furnish details of its grievance redressal mechanism available to producers, OTT platforms and law-enforcement agencies, and to submit an Action Taken Report within 15 days outlining the measures implemented to prevent and remove piracy-related material.

The notice signals a shift towards greater platform accountability rather than relying solely on individual takedown requests. The government has previously acted against more than 3,000 Telegram channels allegedly carrying pirated content.

The development comes amid increasing scrutiny of digital platforms over content regulation and compliance. Telegram was also temporarily blocked in India until June 22 in connection with concerns surrounding the NEET-UG re-examination process following allegations of a paper leak and a subsequent investigation by the Central Bureau of Investigation.

Statement : Shutting down Telegram is a band aid solution and is a disproportionate answer to exam fraud

The Internet Freedom Foundation objects to the directions announced today in the National Testing Agency's press release on action against the Telegram platform. On the NTA's recommendation, the Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology has, under Section 69A of the Information Technology Act, 2000, restricted access to the whole of Telegram in India until 22 June 2026, and has separately ordered the platform to switch off message-editing for every Indian user until 30 June 2026. This is a blunt, nationwide measure aimed at the conduct of rampant fraud rackets, and on the Government's own admission is constitutionally incompatible.

At the outset it is important to note that Section 69A and the Blocking Rules of 2009 framed under it allow the Government to block access to specific “information” on a computer resource. They do not extend to switching off an entire intermediary, still less to ordering a company to redesign its product by removing a feature for a whole country. In Shreya Singhal v Union of India, the Supreme Court upheld Section 69A because it is narrow and hedged with procedural safeguards. Reading it to authorise shutting down a platform that lakhs use is an overbroad restriction by the NTAs own admission. For the message-editing direction the release identifies no source of power at all. If one exists, the order must say so.

The release argues against itself

A restriction on access has to be the least intrusive measure that achieves its aim as per the constitutional test of proportionality laid down in Justice K.S. Puttaswamy v. Union of India (2017) and applied in Anuradha Bhasin v. Union of India (2020). The NTA's own narration shows the block fails its nodal agency, the release says, “has secured the prompt take-down of a substantial number of Telegram channels, groups and bots”, and this targeted work “is the reason the harm caused by these rackets has been contained to the extent it has”. If channel level takedown contained the harm, the case for a blanket block collapses and hence the Government has reached for a heavier tool while conceding that a lighter one was working. The collateral cost sits on the record too as noted in the press release. The block, the NTA accepts, “affects lakhs of citizens who use the Telegram platform for legitimate personal, educational, professional and informational purposes”. The release also says there is "no such paper available outside the secured examination chain" and that “the security of the examination is unaffected by the action taken”. If the exam is secure and no leak exists, what is being suppressed is rumour, and rumour cannot justify closing a platform when specific blocking and criminal prosecution remain available.

Students use of Telegram

The block of telegram is reactive and ineffective and will punish ordinary users instead of addressing the systemic source of exam leaks. This blocking comes in the final days of NEET preparation, when thousands of students depend on Telegram for study groups, doubt-clearing, and shared resources. Also, it is important to consider that the source of exam papers leak will occur from inside the system, among insiders and across the printing and logistics chain, with the platform being the most downstream channel for distribution. Hence, switching off Telegram, is merely a deflection from the repeated failures that will continue while media attention is directed towards this Telegram ban.

Lack of transparency

At present only a press release from the NTA has been provided, which recommended the block but the reasoned order of MeitY, the authority that issued it, has not been released. The Anuradha Bhasin decision requires that orders restricting access be published so they can be tested in court. Here the order, and the reasoning of the committee behind it, stay out of view, and we do not know whether Telegram was heard at all. An announcement of a block is no substitute for an order the affected party can challenge.
Blunt to enforce and very easy to evade
Usually, app-level blocks run through IS-level DNS and IP filtering. They are over inclusive, sweeping in lawful use, yet simple to evade as a determined exam leak racket moves to a VPN or a mirror within minutes while ordinary users lose the service for a week.

We ask the Government to:

1) Publish the MeitY Section 69A order and the NTA recommendation behind it, with reasons;
2) State the legal basis for the message editing direction, or withdraw it;
3) Confirm whether Telegram was given a hearing under the Blocking Rules, and place the committee's record before any court that hears a challenge; and
4) Lift the platform-wide restriction and rely on the targeted takedowns the NTA itself credits with containing the harm.

We emphasise that the NEET (UG) 2026 re-examination is worth protecting and it concerns the future of lakhs of aspirants. It requires securing the entire process of examination rather than reaching for purported band aid solutions that instead cause more harm. The State cannot switch off a service used by lakhs to answer the wrongdoing of a few, and cannot do it through an order no one affected is allowed to read. On its own facts, the Government has done both.

New Delhi, 16 June 2026.

مقاله - ارزش‌های پایه در فرهنگ مجاهدین: نفی خودپرستی و فردیت فروبرنده
مسئله «خودپرستی» یا «ایگوئیسم» در تاریخ فلسفه همواره یکی از موانع اصلی در مسیر تحقق آزادی و عدالت دانسته شده است. افلاطون در جمهوری استدلال می‌کرد که جامعه‌ای که اعضایش فقط در پی منافع شخصی باشند، به فساد و بی‌عدالتی کشیده می‌شود.[۱] ارسطو نیز در اخلاق نیکوماخوس بر این باور بود که فضیلت تنها در تعادل میان خواست‌های فردی و خیر عمومی معنا می‌یابد.[۲]

در دوران مدرن، توماس هابز تصویر انسان را به‌مثابه موجودی خودخواه و منفعت‌طلب ارائه داد که برای رهایی از «جنگ همه علیه همه» ناچار به پذیرش قرارداد اجتماعی است.[۳] شایان ذکر است که ژان ژاک روسو نیز بر آن بود که خودپرستی محصول مناسبات اجتماعی ناعادلانه است و تنها در بستر «اراده عمومی» می‌توان بر آن غلبه کرد.[۴]

این بحث در سنت فلسفه قاره‌ای نیز ادامه یافت. کی‌یرکگور و نیچه هر دو به شیوه‌ای متفاوت بر این نکته تأکید داشتند که خودپرستی، نوعی اسارت درونی است که مانع تحقق «خود اصیل» می‌شود. از دید نیچه، غلبه بر نفس خویش شرط آفرینندگی و فراروی از انسان موجود است.[۵]

خودپرستی در روان‌شناسی و روان‌کاوی
در روان‌شناسی، خودپرستی به‌عنوان گرایشی طبیعی در انسان شناخته شده، اما در صورت افراط، به اختلالات شخصیتی منجر می‌شود. فروید معتقد بود که «خود بزرگ‌شده» (ego inflated) ریشه بسیاری از تعارضات روانی و اجتماعی است.[۶] آدلر نیز بر این نکته تأکید می‌کرد که میل به «برتری‌طلبی» در صورتی که به همبستگی اجتماعی پیوند نخورد، به خودشیفتگی و سلطه‌گری بدل خواهد شد.[۷]

کارل یونگ در تحلیل خود از «سایه» نشان داد که خودپرستی اغلب در قالب انکار ضعف‌ها و فرافکنی بر دیگران ظاهر می‌شود.[۸] روان‌شناسی معاصر نیز، به‌ویژه در مطالعات مربوط به «خودشیفتگی مرضی» (pathological narcissism)، بر این نکته انگشت می‌گذارد که فردیت‌گرایی افراطی نه تنها سلامت فرد، بلکه انسجام اجتماعی را نیز تهدید می‌کند.[۹]

نقد جامعه‌شناختی فردیت‌گرایی
از منظر جامعه‌شناسی، فردیت‌گرایی محصول تحولات مدرن است. ماکس وبر در تحلیل سرمایه‌داری این گزاره را برجسته می‌کند که عقلانیت ابزاری، افراد را به کنشگرانی منفعت‌جو و محاسبه‌گر بدل کرده است.[۱۰] امیل دورکیم نیز هشدار می‌دهد که فردیت‌گرایی افراطی می‌تواند به «آنومی» یا بی‌هنجاری اجتماعی منجر شود؛ وضعیتی که در آن پیوندهای همبستگی از میان می‌رود.[۱۱]

در سنت انتقادی، هربرت مارکوزه و مکتب فرانکفورت تأکید کردند که نظام سرمایه‌داری با ترویج فردگرایی مصرفی، انسان‌ها را از پیوندهای رهایی‌بخش جمعی محروم می‌سازد.[۱۲] زیگمونت باومن نیز در توصیف «مدرنیته سیال» خاطرنشان می‌سازد که فردگرایی امروز به بی‌ثباتی هویت و فروپاشی همبستگی‌های پایدار منجر شده است.[۱۳]

نفی خودپرستی در تجربه‌ی مجاهدین خلق
سازمان مجاهدین خلق در بازخوانی ارزش‌های انسانی، نفی خودپرستی را به‌عنوان گامی اساسی برای رهایی فردی و اجتماعی تعریف می‌کند. در تجربه‌ی آنان، خودپرستی یا «فردیت فروبرنده» فقط یک گرایش فردی نیست، بلکه بازتاب مناسبات قدرت استبدادی و طبقاتی در درون فرد است. بنابراین، غلبه بر نفس به معنای رهایی از بازتولید همان ساختارهای سلطه در سطح شخصی است.

این نگرش را می‌توان با دیدگاه پاولو فریره در آموزش ستمدیدگان مقایسه کرد؛ جایی که او بر ضرورت «رهایی از درونی‌سازی ستمگر» تأکید می‌کند.[۱۴] در عمل، مجاهدین خلق با ترویج فرهنگ جمع‌گرایی و مسئولیت‌پذیری مشترک، کوشیده‌اند بر گرایش‌های فردیت‌گرایانه و خودمحور غلبه کنند.

انقلاب درونی مجاهدین اگر چه با زدودن اندیشه‌ی جنسیت‌گرایی آغاز شد ولی در این نقطه متوقف نماند، در گام‌های بعدی فردیت فروبرنده و واپسگرا هدف قرار گرفت. این جنس از فردیت که باز محصول یک جامعه‌ی طبقاتی است، در تشکیلات انقلابی به عوارضی مانند برتری‌طلبی، خودبزرگ‌بینی، کرسی‌خواهی، دریغ‌کردن از فداکاری، ریختن ثمره‌ی تلاش دیگران به جیب خود منجر می‌شود.

اگر تاریخچه‌ی جنبش‌های انقلابی را مطالعه کنیم، می‌بینیم که چشم‌پوشی از این عارضه هولناک باعث شکست و ناکامی‌های بسیار شده است. تشکیلات انقلابی مجاهدین در بستر یک مبارزه جمعی با کوچک‌ترین نمود فردیت فروبرنده می‌جنگد و مانع از شکل‌گیری و متورم‌شدن آن می‌گردد. این جنگ بیش و پیش از هر چیز با نقد خود همراه است.

مبارزه با فردیت فروبرنده، شخصیت حقیقی و فردیت فرابرنده‌ی انسان را بارز و بارزتر می‌کند. کسی که در پی منافع حقیر شخصی نباشد و حب جاه و مقام او را درنرباید، برای پیشبرد مسئولیت‌های انقلابی قابل اتکا و اعتماد است. تنها و تنها در سایه‌ی چنین مبارزه‌‌ای است که می‌توان به آینده‌ای تابناک در پس این شب اهریمنی باور داشت و ایمان آورد که انقلاب دموکراتیک مردم ایران این‌بار به‌سرقت نخواهد رفت و خمینی دیگری سربرنخواهد کرد تا آن را به سرقت ببرد.

در پرتو مناسبات عاری از حب جاه و مقام است که روابط خواهرانه و برادرانه در بین مجاهدین ساری و جاری شده و می‌شود. انقلاب ایدئولوژیک در مراحل پیشرفته‌اش این روابط را بیش‌از‌پیش صیقل می‌زند و ارتقا می‌دهد.

نمونه‌های تاریخی از نفی خودپرستی
جنبش‌های آزادی‌بخش در سراسر جهان نیز بر نفی خودپرستی به‌عنوان شرط رهایی تأکید کرده‌اند. ماندلا در خاطرات خود می‌نویسد که مقاومت تنها زمانی موفق خواهد بود که افراد منافع شخصی خود را فدای خیر جمعی کنند.[۱۵] گاندی نیز در اصل «آپریگراها» (فقدان دلبستگی به خود) تأکید داشت که مبارز نمی‌تواند در پی منافع شخصی باشد، بلکه باید حقیقت و خیر عمومی را محور قرار دهد.[۱۶]

نفی خودپرستی و فردیت‌ فروبرنده، فراتر از یک توصیه اخلاقی، راهبردی برای تحقق آزادی فردی و اجتماعی است. این نفی به معنای نابودی شخصیت حقیقی و هویت بی‌همتای فرد یا «فردیت فرابرنده» نیست، ارتقاء فردیت به سطحی است که در خدمت آزادی جمعی قرار گیرد. تجربه تاریخی مجاهدین اثبات می‌کند که تنها از رهگذر رهایی از نفس و خودمحوری است که می‌توان به همبستگی واقعی، مقاومت پایدار و جامعه‌ای آزاد دست یافت.

You cannot delete another person’s Reel, geo-block a URL in India, or mass-remove content. There is no public endpoint for that. App Review will not give it to you.

What IE described is a private government–platform pipe, authorised officers put URLs on Sahyog under IT Act 79(3)(b). Meta’s internal compliance stack restricts those URLs, usually for India, under the 3-hour rule. Court filings called this “API-based integration.” Same English word. Not the same API. You cannot call it with an access token.

Also sloppy on units:
  
1.95 lakh is orders, not posts. One order can cover many URLs.

PIB later said ~2.98 lakh URLs. Different count.

“Blocked from Instagram” is often geo-restriction in India, not a global delete. Users have seen Account Status say the post meets Community Standards while India still can’t open it. That is local-law restriction, not Meta’s spam model.

So government notices at this volume + a machine path to meet a 3-hour deadline = a real policy story.

“An AI can automatically block Instagram content with the Meta API” = false. That capability is not in the developer docs, and treating Sahyog as Graph API is how this thread oversells the tech.

If the claim is “takedowns scaled up,” argue that with orders vs URLs and 79(3)(b) vs 69A. Don’t sell it as a public API anyone can point at a meme.

text:
Illegal Infiltration & Fake Documentation:-A Real Case I Handled

Home Minister @AmitShah ji has held that the population of Muslims in India has increased due to illegal infiltration. Let me share a real case I personally handled about 5–6 years ago in Mumbai, one among many that reveal how deep this problem runs. Please do read to understand the rot.

1. The Client’s Request:- One evening after court hours, a Muslim gentleman known to me came to my office. He had given his premises in Govandi, Mumbai, on a leave and license agreement to a family of 6/7 people.
Even after the agreement expired, the family refused to vacate.

I perused his papers and assured him of appropriate legal action. He then asked if the matter could be resolved sooner than usual.
When I explained that such cases typically take little time, he hesitated and what he said next stunned me.

2. The Shocking Revelation :- He quietly said, “Sir, those tenants are not Indians, they are Bangladeshis.”

That single sentence changed everything. Two thoughts struck me instantly:
1. Why hadn’t he mentioned this earlier?
2. How did they even get valid Aadhaar and PAN cards as visible in the agreement?

3. The Investigation:- On examining the documents, everything looked perfectly legitimate; Aadhaar, PAN, ration card, even voter ID.
We filed RTIs, involved the local police, and began to dig deeper.

Gradually, the truth surfaced, the birth certificate forming the basis of all these documents was forged.

Using that single forged certificate from 1967, the accused had created a full legal identity for himself and his family, including Aadhaar, PAN, ration card, and voter ID.

4. A Web of Fraud:- It didn’t stop there. The man had used the same method to obtain documents for his wife and children. His son was even married to an Indian Muslim woman, effectively merging into the Indian population.

During the investigation, we uncovered an organized network, a full-fledged industry operating to regularize illegal immigrants by manufacturing fake Indian identities that pass every verification test.

5. The Larger Problem:-India’s diversity makes such infiltration even easier. People entering from Bangladesh, Pakistan, Myanmar, or Nepal often resemble locals making visual identification almost impossible.

Add to this the corruption that exists from border checkpoints to administrative offices, and you have a perfect ecosystem for illegal population growth.

In this very case, we found the involvement of certain officials, and shockingly, even a few lawyers.

6. A Moment That Exposed the Rot:- One of those lawyers, representing the Bangladeshi accused, told my Muslim junior,
“How can you do this? This is a matter of religion.”
My junior stood firm and warned him of a complaint before the Bar Council.

This single moment revealed how some individuals, blinded by religious or political motives, are actively protecting those who illegally enter and settle in India.

7. The Unanswered Question:- 
This wasn’t the only case, I have come across several similar ones.
Despite being aware of this menace for years, successive governments have failed to implement a robust national mechanism to identify and deport such individuals.

8. The Hope:- Now that the Home Minister himself has spoken openly about the issue, one can only hope it translates into real, concrete action. India needs a firm, technology-backed, corruption-proof mechanism to detect and remove non-Indians living here on forged documents.

Illegal infiltration is not just a demographic concern, it’s a threat to national integrity, law, and fairness. The time for acknowledgment is over.
The time for action has arrived.

@AmitShahOffice
